content: A sanatorium, also referred to as a sanitarium or sanitorium, is a medical facility specifically designed for the treatment of long-term illnesses, most notably tuberculosis. Historically, a distinction was sometimes made between a sanitarium, which was considered a type of health resort (such as the Battle Creek Sanitarium), and a sanatorium, which functioned more as a hospital. The Saskatchewan Lung Association notes that when the National Anti-Tuberculosis Association was established in 1904, there was a deliberate effort to differentiate between familiar health resorts and the newly emerging tuberculosis treatment hospitals. To emphasize the scientific approach to healing and treatment, the term sanatorium was coined, derived from the Latin verb root sano, meaning to heal, rather than the Latin noun sanitas, meaning health. Before the advent of antibiotics, the rationale behind sanatoriums was that rest and proper nutrition provided the best opportunity for a patient’s immune system to contain and isolate pockets of pulmonary tuberculosis infection. In the early 20th century, tuberculosis sanatoriums were widespread in the United States. Notable examples include the Piedmont Sanatorium in Burkeville, Virginia, which was the first tuberculosis sanatorium for Black patients, and the Waverly Hills Sanatorium in Louisville, Kentucky, established in 1911. The G. Holley Hospital in Lantana, Florida, remains the last freestanding tuberculosis sanatorium in the United States. Switzerland was home to numerous sanatoriums, as the clean mountain air was believed to be highly beneficial for treating lung diseases. Patients from across Europe were sent there to recover. For instance, the Heliantia Sanatorium in Valadares, Portugal, was dedicated to treating bone tuberculosis from the 1930s to the 1960s. The discovery of streptomycin in 1943 by Albert Schatz, a graduate student at Rutgers University, marked the first true cure for tuberculosis. This breakthrough led to the gradual closure of sanatoriums. By the 1950s, tuberculosis was no longer a significant public health threat, and most sanatoriums ceased operations. Many were demolished, though some were repurposed for modern medical uses. For example, the Tambaram Sanatorium in South India is now a center of excellence for AIDS treatment, and the state hospital in Sanatorium, Mississippi, has been converted into a regional mental retardation center. In the former Soviet Union, the term sanatorium had a slightly different connotation, referring to a hybrid facility combining a resort or recreational center with a medical institution. These facilities were intended to provide short-term, comprehensive rest and medical care. In literature, sanatoriums have also served as significant settings. Thomas Mann’s novel The Magic Mountain (Der Zauberberg), one of the most influential works of the 20th century, is set in a sanatorium. Mann drew inspiration from personal experience, as his wife was hospitalized for several months in 1912 at Dr. Friedrich Jessen’s Waldsanatorium in Davos, Switzerland. The Magic Mountain was first published in two volumes by S. Fischer Verlag in 1924.
